text: In 1977, Minah Bte Gap and her husband Rani Bin Omar were resettled from Pulau Semakau to a one-room rental flat at Telok Blangah, on the Singapore mainland.
"Our hearts are attached to the island," she said.
Kanwaljit Soin, a Nominated Member of Parliament, appealed for Seking to be excluded on heritage grounds.
The appeal was refused: keeping the little island out of the scheme would have cost another 130 million Singapore dollars for an alternative site.
Lorong Halus itself closed on the 31st of March 1999, completely full.
Semakau Landfill opened the next morning.

The design was simple to describe and enormous to do: a seven-kilometre wall of rock — a perimeter bund — drawn through the sea between Pulau Semakau and Pulau Seking, enclosing 350 hectares of water.
On the agency's 2019 figures the island receives about 2,100 tonnes a day — some 1,500 tonnes of incineration ash and 600 tonnes of non-incinerable waste, about 700,000 tonnes a year.
Healthy mangroves growing hard against the bund are taken as living evidence that the liners beneath are not leaking.
The landfill's first alarm system is a forest.
Giant clams, including the endangered fluted giant clam, live on the reef; so do seahorses, turtles and reef sharks, with dolphins and otters in the waters around.
They had to rescue a reef from the rubbish island's own lagoon before they could bury it.
At current filling rates, the expectation now is that Semakau will be full by about 2035.
Some of it is already under Singaporeans' feet.
The road sections opened to traffic in April 2022, and the ash has performed comparably to conventional material.

In June 2026 the newest institution arrived: TREASURES, a national research centre for residue and toxic waste, funded with 35 million Singapore dollars, set up by the environment agency and the university, with a whole division devoted to the landfill's transformation — recovering, treating and repurposing what has been sent to Semakau, and what is already stored there.
In June 2025 the organisation held the first Hari Orang Pulau, Islanders' Day, at West Coast Park, reuniting the families of islands most Singaporeans have never heard of.
"Our hearts are attached to the island."
